content: Apnoea of prematurity (AoP) is characterized by a cessation of breathing lasting 20 seconds or more in preterm infants. It can also be defined as a shorter pause in breathing if it is accompanied by bradycardia (a slow heart rate) and hypoxaemia (low oxygen levels in the blood). There is evidence suggesting that the severity of AoP may be linked to delays in neurodevelopment. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is a non-invasive method of providing ventilatory support that has been shown to be relatively safe and effective in managing respiratory distress in preterm infants. However, its safety and efficacy in preventing and treating AoP remain uncertain. The primary objectives of this review were to evaluate the effects of CPAP on AoP in preterm infants, comparing it to either supportive care or mechanical ventilation, and to assess the impact of different CPAP delivery systems on AoP in this population. A systematic search was conducted in September 2022 across several databases, including the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL. Additional searches were performed in clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant studies. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the use of CPAP for AoP in preterm infants born before 37 weeks of gestation. Cross-over studies were also included if sufficient data were available for analysis. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis. This included independent risk of bias assessments and data extraction by at least two authors, with discrepancies resolved by a third author. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of evidence for key outcomes, including CPAP failure, apnoea frequency, and adverse effects of CPAP. The review included four single-center trials conducted in Malaysia, Spain, Germany, and North America, involving a total of 138 preterm infants with a mean or median gestational age of 26 to 28 weeks. Two of the studies were parallel-group RCTs, while the other two were cross-over trials. None of the studies compared CPAP to supportive care alone. Instead, all trials compared different types of CPAP devices. Two studies compared variable flow CPAP devices to ventilator CPAP, one compared two different variable flow devices, and one compared a variable flow device to bubble CPAP. The interventions were administered for durations ranging from six to 48 hours, with CPAP pressures set between 4 and 6 cm H2O. All trials were assessed as having a high risk of bias due to inadequate blinding of participants and personnel. Two studies also had a high risk of bias for blinding of outcome assessors. Additionally, two cross-over studies were at high risk of carry-over effects due to insufficient washout periods, and one study used an analysis method that was not widely accepted for cross-over designs. In the comparison of CPAP to supportive care alone, no studies were identified for inclusion. For the comparison of variable flow CPAP to ventilator CPAP, two studies were included. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it remains unclear whether there is any difference in the incidence of CPAP failure, defined as the need for mechanical ventilation (risk ratio [RR] 0.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.01 to 2.90; 1 study, 26 participants). Similarly, it is uncertain whether there is any difference in the frequency of apnoea events (mean difference [MD] per four-hour interval -0.10, 95% CI -1.30 to 1.10; 1 study, 26 participants). Adverse events and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not adequately reported. In the comparison of variable flow CPAP to bubble CPAP, one study was included, but it did not report the pre-specified outcomes of interest. For the comparison of Infant Flow variable flow CPAP to Medijet variable flow CPAP, one study involving 80 participants was included. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is unclear whether there is any difference in the incidence of CPAP failure (RR 2.62, 95% CI 0.91 to 7.53). The frequency of apnoea events was not reported, and the study did not provide information on adverse events or neurodevelopmental outcomes. No studies were identified for the comparison of CPAP to mechanical ventilation. In conclusion, the available evidence is limited and of very low certainty. It remains unclear whether any specific CPAP device is more effective than other forms of supportive care, other CPAP devices, or mechanical ventilation for the prevention and treatment of AoP in preterm infants. The devices evaluated in the included studies were variable flow CPAP, bubble CPAP, and ventilator CPAP. Each comparison was based on data from a single study, and there are theoretical reasons to believe that different devices may have varying effects on AoP. Further research is needed to clarify these uncertainties.
